The ending of the story feels completely natural and earned because it brings Clara's character arc and the central themes of the narrative to a satisfying resolution. Throughout the story, Clara is trying to assemble a fake, sophisticated persona to impress her pretentious housemates—metaphorically "building a chair to impress the neighbors." The climax exposes the hollowness of her housemates and her own efforts. The ending provides a strong sense of closure: by retrieving her scarf, feeling nothing toward Carl and Martin, laying down a newspaper from her actual hometown (*Cleveland Plain Dealer*), and engaging in the practical, unglamorous task of greasing her boots to join the grounded Johan, Clara finally abandons her pretentious "auditions" in favor of authenticity. Everything in the piece builds toward this quiet moment of self-acceptance.
